chunks.title: Alla Prima Technique
chunks.content: Alla prima, Italian for at the first attempt, describes the technique of completing an oil painting in a single session while the paint remains wet. The technique requires a properly prepared ground — typically a toned imprimatura of burnt sienna, raw umber, or a warm gray — so the painter is laying color relationships rather than searching for them. The brushwork is loaded, the marks are committed, and there is minimal reworking. Alla prima depends on the fat-over-lean rule: lean mixtures (more solvent, less oil) go down first, fatter mixtures (more oil, less solvent) on top, so the lower layers dry faster than the upper layers and the paint film does not crack. The hallmark of an alla prima picture is the freshness of the edges — crisp where decisive, lost where the artist changed their mind, never overworked. Palette-knife ridges, gestural streaks radiating outward, scraped dragged smeared paint are all signatures. The technique is incompatible with slow-drying pigments like raw umber under fast-drying layers. When prompting a reference generator for alla prima, name the single-session commitment and the gestural stroke vocabulary.

chunks.title: Glazing and Velatura
chunks.content: Glazing, also called velatura when applied as a tinted film, is the technique of laying thin, transparent layers of oil paint over a dried underpainting. The underpainting is typically a value study in grisaille or a monochrome imprimatura; the glazes supply the chroma and the temperature. Because each glaze is transparent, the layers optically mix in the viewer's eye rather than on the palette. The technique depends on the slow drying of oil and the use of translucent pigments: madder lake, alizarin crimson, indigo, viridian, raw umber, yellow ochre, and the quinacridones. Opaque pigments like cadmium yellow, lead white, and titanium white cannot be glazed because they obscure the layers beneath. Glazes are typically bound in a lean medium — a touch of linseed oil with a larger proportion of solvent — to avoid cracking. The technique produces a depth of color unmatched by direct painting: a glazed red has an internal glow that a directly-applied red cannot match. When prompting a reference generator, name the glazing commitment and the translucent pigment vocabulary.

chunks.title: Scumbling
chunks.content: Scumbling is the technique of dragging a relatively dry, opaque or semi-opaque layer of paint over a dried underpainting so that the underlayer shows through the broken, irregular film. The technique is the opposite of glazing: scumbling adds broken light and atmospheric diffusion rather than transparent depth. The brush is loaded with paint that has had much of its oil removed, often by wiping on a rag, so the paint goes down as a broken crust. Scumbled passages are typically cooler than the underlying warm layer, producing optical grays and muted violets that cannot be premixed on the palette. The technique is associated with Rembrandt, Turner, and the late Monet, all of whom used scumbling to soften transitions and to suggest atmosphere. Scumbling depends on a sufficiently dried underlayer; applying scumble to wet paint produces mud. The hallmark of a good scumble is the legibility of the underlayer through the broken film. When prompting a reference generator, name the broken-film scumble and the atmospheric diffusion.

chunks.title: Impasto
chunks.content: Impasto is the technique of applying oil paint thickly enough that the brush or palette-knife marks stand in relief from the canvas. The paint is loaded heavily, often with stiff bristle brushes or a palette knife, and laid down in confident strokes that preserve the gesture of the mark. Impasto can be applied alla prima over a long session, or built up over many sessions with each layer preserving the evidence of the previous stroke. The technique is associated with Rembrandt, Van Gogh, Frank Auerbach, and Leon Kossoff. Impasto is incompatible with fast-drying acrylic paint; oil's slow drying time and its body when loaded are essential. The hallmark of impasto is the autonomy of the stroke: each mark is a self-contained event that catches real light from its physical surface. Impasto passages read as the painter's most committed and physically present marks; they are the parts of the picture that exist most strongly in three dimensions. When prompting a reference generator, name the impasto build-up and the gestural stroke vocabulary.

chunks.title: Sgraffito
chunks.content: Sgraffito is the technique of scratching through a dried upper layer of paint to reveal a differently-colored layer beneath. The technique requires an underlayer that is thoroughly dry and an upper layer that is dry enough to scratch cleanly without smearing. The tool is typically the butt end of a brush, a palette knife, or a stylus. Sgraffito is associated with the Venetian Renaissance, particularly Titian and Veronese, who used it to add highlights to drapery and to suggest the weave of fabric by scratching pale lines through a darker top layer. The technique is also used in expressionist painting to add graphic marks — branches against a sky, rigging against a hull — that integrate with the painted surface rather than sitting on top of it. Sgraffito depends on the difference in value or chroma between the two layers: a light reveal through a dark top layer reads as a highlight; a dark reveal through a light top layer reads as a graphic accent. When prompting a reference generator, name the scratched reveal and the value contrast between the layers.

chunks.title: Dry-Brush
chunks.content: Dry-brush is the technique of applying oil paint with a brush that has had most of its paint removed, so only a faint broken film of pigment transfers to the canvas. The brush is loaded and then wiped on a rag or scraped against the palette edge until it holds barely any paint. The marks that result are irregular, broken, and broken-edged, preserving the texture of both the brush and the underlying surface. Dry-brush is used to suggest rough textures — weathered wood, coarse fabric, foliage, distant terrain — where a fully-loaded stroke would read as too solid. The technique depends on a textured ground or a previously dried impasto surface that can catch the broken pigment. Dry-brush is incompatible with smooth grounds; on a slick imprimatura the brush slips and the broken effect is lost. The hallmark of dry-brush is the suggestion of texture rather than the description of it. When prompting a reference generator, name the broken-edge texture and the underlying surface.

chunks.title: Fat-over-Lean Rule
chunks.content: The fat-over-lean rule is the foundational structural principle of oil painting: each successive layer of paint should contain more oil (fatter) than the layer beneath it (leaner). The rule exists because oil paint dries through oxidation of its oil binder, and an oil-rich layer over an oil-poor layer dries from the top down. A layer that dries from the bottom up, which would happen with a lean layer over a fat layer, shrinks unevenly and cracks. The rule is implemented by starting with lean mixtures — paint thinned with solvent, with little or no added medium — and progressing to fatter mixtures — paint with added linseed oil, walnut oil, or a commercial medium like Liquin or Oleogel. The progression matches the painter's deepening commitment: lean imprimatura, lean underpainting, fatter mid-tones, fattest highlights and accents. The rule is incompatible with reworking a lean passage with a fat brush; the lean paint smears. When prompting a reference generator, name the fat-over-lean progression and the medium commitment.

chunks.title: Slow vs Fast Drying Pigments
chunks.content: Pigments differ dramatically in how quickly they dry, and the painter must plan layers accordingly. Slow driers include raw umber, burnt umber, ivory black, and the quinacridones; these can take days or weeks to dry thoroughly. Fast driers include lead white, flake white, the cadmiums, and cobalt blue; these may dry overnight under proper conditions. The rule is that slow driers should never be applied under fast driers — the lower layer will still be wet when the upper layer dries, leading to uneven drying and eventual cracking. The exception is when the slow-drier layer is applied so thin (a glaze or imprimatura) that its slow drying is not a problem. Pigments also differ in transparency: the earths and lakes are typically transparent; the cadmiums, lead white, and most manufactured pigments are typically opaque. The painter's choice of pigment ordering determines the speed of execution: a slow-drier underpainting supports a longer painting process; a fast-drier underpainting supports a faster, more alla-prima approach. When prompting a reference generator, name the slow-drier/fast-drier ordering.

chunks.title: Transparent vs Opaque Pigments
chunks.content: Pigments fall into two broad classes for the oil painter: transparent and opaque. Transparent pigments — alizarin crimson, madder lake, indigo, viridian, raw umber, yellow ochre, the quinacridones — allow light to pass through them and reflect off the layers beneath, producing a depth of color unmatched by opaque pigments. They are the workhorses of glazing. Opaque pigments — lead white, titanium white, the cadmiums, chrome yellow, cobalt blue — scatter light back to the viewer and obscure the layers beneath. They are the workhorses of direct painting and impasto. A third class, semi-opaque or sedimentary pigments — terre verte, Venetian red, some yellow ochres — sits between, allowing some light to pass while still building up body. The painter's choice between transparent and opaque determines whether a passage reads as luminous or as solid. Glazing requires transparent pigments; scumbling often uses opaque or semi-opaque pigments over a dried ground. When prompting a reference generator, name the transparency choice and the resulting optical effect.

chunks.title: Sedimentary Earth Pigments
chunks.content: The sedimentary earth pigments — yellow ochre, raw sienna, burnt sienna, raw umber, burnt umber, terre verte — are among the oldest and most reliable in the oil painter's palette. Mined from natural deposits, they are typically semi-opaque or transparent, slow-drying, and extremely stable in mixtures. They are the workhorses of the underpainting and the muted portions of any picture: the warm shadow on a wall, the cool green of a distant hill, the brown of a wooden floor. Because they are inexpensive, lightfast, and mix cleanly, they form the foundation of any disciplined palette. The earths also serve as 'bridging' pigments: they harmonize mixtures that would otherwise clash. A mixture of cadmium red and viridian is jarring; a mixture of cadmium red and terre verte is balanced. When prompting a reference generator for a grounded palette, name the earth pigment vocabulary and the harmonizing role they play.

chunks.title: Warm-Cool Contrast
chunks.content: Warm-cool contrast is the fundamental structural principle of oil painting color. Warm colors — cadmium red, cadmium yellow, burnt sienna, Naples yellow, vermillion — advance toward the viewer and read as active. Cool colors — cobalt blue, viridian, cerulean, Payne's gray, ultramarine — recede from the viewer and read as passive. The contrast is not absolute: a cool color sits beside a still-cooler color and reads as warm by comparison. The painter exploits warm-cool contrast to model form, to establish focal hierarchy, to push planes into depth, and to bind a composition's color scheme together. A portrait typically has warm flesh against cool background; a landscape typically has warm foreground against cool distance. The principle is independent of value: a cool light and a warm shadow are just as readable as the more conventional warm-light-cool-shadow pairing. The painter should also manage the chroma of the contrast: muted warms against muted cools read as atmospheric; saturated warms against muted cools read as dramatic. When prompting a reference generator, name the warm-cool contrast and its role in the composition.

chunks.title: Complementary Pairs
chunks.content: Complementary pairs — red-green, blue-orange, yellow-violet — sit opposite each other on the color wheel and produce the strongest possible chromatic contrast. In oil painting, complementary contrast is used to make a passage vibrate with energy: a small dose of cadmium red placed beside a viridian green makes both colors appear more saturated than they would alone. The complementary relationship is also a tool for neutralizing: mixing complementary colors produces grays and browns that are richer than the muddy grays obtained by mixing black and white. The painter uses complementary contrast to establish focal hierarchy (a saturated complement draws the eye), to model form (warm flesh against cool green shadow), and to balance the overall color scheme (a composition heavy on yellows needs violets to feel resolved). The principle is distinct from simultaneous contrast, where complementary colors placed side by side enhance each other without being mixed. When prompting a reference generator, name the complementary pair and the role it plays in the composition.

chunks.title: Support and Ground Preparation
chunks.content: The support — canvas, linen, panel — and its ground preparation are foundational to the oil painting's long-term stability and immediate working properties. Linen, woven from flax, is preferred over cotton for its strength and its subtle surface texture; it is typically stretched over a wooden frame and sized with rabbit-skin glue or an acrylic medium. The ground is the layer applied over the support to seal it and to provide a working surface. Traditional grounds include the chalk-and-glue gesso, the oil-based lead-white ground, and the toned imprimatura — a thin wash of oil paint, typically burnt sienna, raw umber, or a warm gray, applied over a white ground to give the painter a middle-value starting point. A toned imprimatura is essential for alla-prima work because it allows the painter to work in both directions from a middle value rather than fighting a stark white ground. Panels — typically plywood or hardwood — are favored for glazing and detail work because they do not flex. When prompting a reference generator, name the support and ground commitment.

chunks.title: Mediums and Solvents
chunks.content: The oil painter's medium — the liquid added to paint to modify its flow, drying time, and gloss — is a fundamental tool. Linseed oil, pressed from flax seeds, is the classic medium: it slows drying, increases gloss, and yellows slightly with age. Walnut oil, pressed from walnuts, is paler and less prone to yellowing; it is favored for whites and pale passages. Poppy oil is the palest and slowest-drying; it is reserved for whites and blues where yellowing would be most damaging. Solvents — mineral spirits, Gamsol, turpentine — are used to thin paint and to clean brushes. The fat-over-lean rule (see oil_painting_style_007) governs medium selection: lean (solvent-rich, oil-poor) for underlayers, fat (oil-rich, solvent-poor) for upper layers. Commercial mediums — Liquin, Oleogel, Gamblin's mediums — combine oils, solvents, and resins to produce specific working properties: faster drying for glazing, slower drying for blending, glossier finish for final layers. When prompting a reference generator, name the medium commitment and the resulting working properties.
